vocab.definition: Basic freedoms and protections for everyone.
Being treated as a person who matters.
Feeling accepted as part of a group.
Treating people and differences with care.
A way to share a view or choice.
Taking account of people’s rights and needs.

cases.text: A meeting takes spoken ideas only. Jo wants to write an idea.
cases.fact: Only one response mode is accepted.
cases.next_step: Offer notes, pointing or another agreed mode.
cases.staff_note: Record which option the learner actually chooses.

cases.text: A notice is hard to read. Lee asks for clear words and pictures.
cases.fact: The notice is not usable for Lee.
cases.next_step: Ask Lee what helps and provide a clear version.
cases.staff_note: Do not assume one format suits everyone.

cases.text: A group laughs at someone’s different belief.
cases.next_step: Stop the mockery and seek staff support for respectful discussion.
cases.staff_note: No pupil must defend or disclose a belief.

cases.text: Two people want different quiet activities for a shared space.
cases.next_step: Listen to both and agree a workable option or turn.
cases.staff_note: Rights do not mean every preference can be met immediately.

cases.text: A person is left out because the usual equipment is hard for them to use.
cases.next_step: Ask them and adapt the equipment, format or role.
cases.staff_note: Do not assign a lesser role without asking the person.

cases.text: Someone says people who break rules no longer have rights.
cases.fact: Rights are treated as a reward.
cases.next_step: Explain that rights belong to everyone.
cases.staff_note: Fair safety rules still apply; avoid promises about specific legal remedies.

B. Human rights belong to everyone; they are not rewards for good behaviour. A setting can address harmful behaviour fairly while treating the person with dignity and respecting others’ rights. Reteach with a calm response to an unsafe action, without denying the person a voice or basic care.
Access and practice
Supported: choose a change for A or B. Independent: explain how it helps someone join. Aspire: compare two views and a fair next step.
Model an accessible way to give an idea. Pupils choose one barrier and proposal, share with a real audience in their chosen mode, hear the reply and record what they would change or keep.

Begin evidence during practice and finish during capture. Accept speech, pointing, drawing, writing or usual AAC. Scribe exact words without supplying the assessed reason. No forced pair work or public performance.
Safe teaching evidence and learner voice
Boundaries

Use fictional settings. Do not require pupils to disclose disability, belief, identity or personal rights concerns. Avoid debates about whether a group deserves rights. Refer real concerns to staff and local procedures.
Assessment and feedback

Credit a concrete barrier and a feasible change that listens to the affected person. Accept plain-word links to dignity, privacy, education or participation without article/criterion numbers. Record the actual classroom audience and response; a proposal is not a claim that a real school policy changed.

Retain actual work, response mode and support. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school's evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only after evidence is banked. Blank forms and adult models are not completed learner evidence.
Lundy moments
Space: calm, accessible participation. Voice: a choice, reason or help request. Audience: the adult listens or reads and replies. Influence: record the support or next-step change made in response.
Speaking listening and writing
Present a proposal, listen to another view and respond with a reason. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio; no communication criteria are assigned here.

Model and hinge

A club is planning a shared activity. Jo wants to give an idea in writing. The organiser accepts notes as well as speech. The group listens without mocking people. They explain what can change and why. Jo checks whether the new option helps.

B. Human rights belong to everyone; they are not rewards for good behaviour. A setting can address harmful behaviour fairly while treating the person with dignity and respecting others’ rights. Reteach with a calm response to an unsafe action, without denying the person a voice or basic care.
Individual evidence key

Credit a concrete barrier and a feasible change that listens to the affected person. Accept plain-word links to dignity, privacy, education or participation without article/criterion numbers. Record the actual classroom audience and response; a proposal is not a claim that a real school policy changed.
Feedback boundaries and next teaching
Card A: Record which option the learner actually chooses.
Card B: Do not assume one format suits everyone.
Card C: No pupil must defend or disclose a belief.
Card D: Rights do not mean every preference can be met immediately.
Card E: Do not assign a lesser role without asking the person.
Card F: Fair safety rules still apply; avoid promises about specific legal remedies.
Common misunderstandings
Rights are not rewards. Fair access need not mean identical support. Respect does not require agreement with every idea, and safety rules can protect everyone’s participation.
Teaching boundary

Use fictional settings. Do not require pupils to disclose disability, belief, identity or personal rights concerns. Avoid debates about whether a group deserves rights. Refer real concerns to staff and local procedures.
Feedback

If a reason is missing, return to the fact or actual work. Re-model a different example, then keep the learner’s own revision. Use NS+ and the learner response in their own colour before R. E means evidence actually banked. Keep safeguarding records separate.
